title: A ? of When with Panda Bear
summary: Pete Kember discusses A ? of When, his collaboration with Panda Bear, Jamaican musical influences and making music with hope for the future. He also reflects on radio and record stores as places to discover music.
transcript:
Pete Kember, Sonic Boom, spoke with Lauren Taylor from Portugal about A Question of When, his second album with Panda Bear. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 23 July 2026.

Lauren: Pete Kember was one of the original co-founders of that highly influential UK band, alongside Jason Pierce, who had a quite famous falling out, the two of them, with the band dissolving in 1991. Famously, Pete Kember and Jason Pierce recorded the tracks from their final record together as Spacemen 3, Recurring, in separate studios, splitting the vinyl down the middle, with one side dedicated to each artist. And, of course, Jason Pierce going on to form Spiritualized. And since Spacemen 3, Pete Kember has really continuously pushed the boundaries under different monikers, like Spectrum and E.A.R. and, of course, as Sonic Boom. He's also been the secret weapon in the producer's chair for massive records by MGMT and Beach House. And, of course, Panda Bear, Noah Lennox from the groundbreaking Animal Collective, who we just heard from earlier. Pete's collaborative partnership with Noah Lennox goes back to 2011, with Pete co-producing Panda Bear's Tomboy record, and also his 2015 release, Panda Bear Meets the Grim Reaper.

The two icons of psychedelic pop are both based in Portugal, Noah for the last two decades, and Pete Kember for over a decade now. And they've combined their brilliant musical minds on two collaborative albums together now, 2022's Reset, and now their most recent offering, called A Question of When, which is an album that famously the band have not made available via streaming services. There's no music videos. It is a very intentional decision by the band to keep things, in their words, IRL rather than URL, with the goal for the music to create physical connections between people, and to encourage them to enjoy a real experience in the world and with each other. The new record, A Question of When, they've said is a deliberate choice to use sounds and textures that they haven't used before, almost as a sonic reset after their Reset record, in a way. It's still another total sonic playground, though. They've packed in everything from Mary Lattimore's harp loops to steel drums to yodelling, and even bits of a mariachi band as well. And while it sounds incredibly dreamy, the tracks are actually diving into some heavy themes, like online exhaustion and climate anxiety as well.

I began the interview by asking Pete Kember if they intentionally leaned on these more uplifting sonic textures to act as more of an optimistic counterweight to the darker subject matter that they're writing about.

Pete: Yeah, absolutely. And it was the same with Reset. We're dealing with some tricky issues in Reset, but it was something that we talked about before starting to work together as Panda Bear and Sonic Boom. I was talking with Noah about how I always was really impressed by Jamaican music from the mid and late 60s, that they were dealing with some super tough issues in Jamaica. Everything was collapsing and crashing. There's just some amazing music that came out of that era, and presented in a very positive way, even though they're talking about not being able to get food, and having massive inflation, where their money's not worth anything. And they're singing songs about these police and thieves. The Junior Murvin track would be a good example. They're talking about tough issues, but in a really beautiful, positive way. So we went into the whole thing of working together with that as one of our touchstones.

Lauren: Would you say the record overall is a hopeful record?

Pete: Yeah, I think you have to be a little realistic when you can look out into the world around you and see what's going on. It's very hard not to let that enter your consciousness, but I think you have to be positive, and be looking for ways that things can be different. Most of the problems on this planet are caused by all of us. And so it's really all of us who have to act if we want to change that and see things different. If we think someone's going to come along and wave a magic wand, God forbid a politician, then, yeah, there is no positivity if you believe that. But if you believe that humans can make good, I think you have to have some positivity.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:40–00:05:35]

Lauren: Keeping the vibe musically positive being a conscious choice, does that joy just happen naturally when you and Noah hang out and create music together?

Pete: Yeah, well, we're trying to amuse and stimulate ourselves, really, and we're sort of indulging each other, really. I make the music, and I make a lot more of it than we use. I make it to find things that inspire him as much as possible, and what he does always inspires me. It's a very easy working relationship with Noah. He's easy to work with. He's very giving. And at the end of the day, if both of us don't like it, if there's anything he doesn't like, I drop it in a flash. It's really important that we both like what we do. We don't really think of it as work and friendship. It's friendship, and we make music within that. But, I mean, we're kind of lucky. I would say I worked hard never to have a real job. But as a musician you're lucky, really, because you are doing what you want to do on your own terms. That might mean you have to eat frozen pizza for a year or two here and there, or in my case a decade or two. But essentially I was happy doing what I wanted to do, so we're very lucky.

Lauren: You've mentioned you're always looking for where there might be a new seam of gold to be mined in terms of your working relationship together. You've mentioned a Goldilocks zone where you can exist nicely. Given how distinct your individual sonic signatures are, what does that Goldilocks zone look like and feel like when you hit the studio and get it just right?

Pete: I don't know. It was an experiment, really, to do this when we started doing the Reset stuff. I wasn't sure quite exactly how it could all work out, but it's just been a very natural thing. I guess the rule of thumb is if we really enjoy it, then possibly other people might, because you never know. Until your record goes out into the world, you have no idea how it could be. And I know I've worked with people like MGMT, who had several big hits, and I remember asking them, did they know? Did you know that was going to be a hit? Did you know 'Kids' was going to be a... They had no idea. In fact, those songs had already been released a year or two earlier, where they had made zero impact. So, yeah, you just don't know with these things.

[Unclear audio at 00:08:13–00:08:31]

Lauren: You said the goal of the music and the campaign rollout of this record is to create that physical connection between people. The press release mentioned IRL, not URL; more rock and roll, not flick and scroll. The aim to be to encourage people to enjoy a real experience in the world and with each other. And yet you famously have made this not available on streaming services, and are keeping everything as offline as possible. Skipping streaming services is a bold move today, and you've mentioned you don't think streaming has been good for culture. What's the biggest piece of culture you feel like we've lost to convenience, and how does this record maybe claw it back?

Pete: I have this theory, and I doubt I'm the originator of it, but my feeling is, to get creative, the first thing you got to do is get bored. And I think once you get bored, that's when your mind starts being creative, and you say, let's form a band, let's write a song, let's... And I think this overly addictive and seductive world that exists in an iPhone, and this is kind of being toxified, I mean intentionally, by the platforms who have done it, it's really not had a good effect on music and art in general, people getting away from having these real-life interactions.

I think the most magical things in life are things that happen when you least expect. You go out into the world with a good frame of mind and meet people, and magic happens. It's not impossible through a screen, but I think you're less likely to get catfished IRL. This is a phenomenon that only exists really through digital platforms and digital messaging and stuff. And I just think it's a much better, really a better interaction. And some of these things, I mean radio being one of them, that have been a little bit overlooked in the streaming era, I think they're a much more interesting way to consume music and do stuff.

Lauren: It's interesting you mentioned radio there. Obviously Triple R, we're celebrating 50 years this year. What is it in particular about radio? How do you view the role of a radio DJ, or the community station, as an alternative to the modern algorithm? What does radio maybe give the listener that a streaming playlist can't?

Pete: Well, personality, for sure. And once you find, I think, a radio station where you like what they do, or you like particular DJs, that you like their thing, it's a magical learning experience. It's a bit like going into a record shop and speaking to the guy who works in there, who has all this knowledge about music but has taste as well, that specific taste. His taste isn't based on what's the most purchased, or the most not purchased. It's not an algorithmic-based thing. I just think it's a much more genuine way to do things, and a nicer interaction, really.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:03–00:12:26]

Lauren: I heard the Unfollow Panda Bear and Sonic Boom campaign backfired for you, Pete. You got more followers than ever in one day, is that right?

Pete: Yeah. I mean, I don't follow anyone. I never did. I followed zero since day one, because I felt like if I was going to follow anyone, I had to follow everyone, and I definitely didn't want to do that. Yeah, it did. It was incredibly popular. It was incredibly successful, that little part of the campaign. Turned out to be part of the campaign, I guess now we'll say, in the rear-view mirror. But yeah, I had more followers coming from that in one day than any other day of doing social media.

[Unclear audio at 00:13:24–00:13:52]

Lauren: I wanted to ask about the artwork as well for the new record. Did that originally come from a drawing you did on the back of a napkin, is that right? That's amazing. That's so cool. I need to screenshot this moment.

Pete: I can send you the picture, but the artwork on the front sleeve is created by Julian House, based on a sketch I did, I think, is probably the fairest way to say it. His rendition of it is a lot better than mine, I have to say.

Lauren: I don't know, it's pretty good. It's pretty similar to the album cover there.

Pete: Yeah. I wanted something really propulsive, and I wanted something that looked like it was in motion, because I think things are seriously in motion. Maybe, I think at this point, probably unstoppably. And I think we're about to see some big changes in society and politics as well. I think things have got to the point where it's not a question of if, it's a question of when. And that was the inspiration for the album title, and that song, 'A Question of When', I think really is the centrepiece of the record, and sort of is what everything else is conversing around, that song.

[Unclear audio at 00:15:35–00:16:31]

Pete: I like working on different things, and with slightly different stylistic things. I don't like to do the same thing the whole time. And when I hear something I really like, I usually try and work with the people if I can. That's how I worked with Iceage or Panda Bear, or, I mean, MGMT and Beach House both approached me, but yeah, I approach people if I like their music, and say, if you fancy trying to do some stuff, let's see what happens. But yeah, we work here just informally, out here in the countryside in Sintra; have an informal studio here. But yeah, it's fun.

[Unclear audio at 00:17:24–00:17:55]

Pete: I think it's like most places: there's a level of enshittification, which I believe is in the dictionary in Australia. It needed a word for that concept. But this is a place that's been — not being improved by influences.

Lauren: You've said Portugal is seductive. Can you tell me a bit more about why you think it's seductive?

Pete: I think it's really magical because it didn't buy into — Portugal was one of the original third-world countries. The original meaning of third-world country was a country that didn't take money from America, first world, or Russia, the second world.

And the fascist dictators they had in Portugal and Spain at that time, Franco and Salazar, who were sort of fascism light, I would say, a little bit, as much as fascism can ever be light, but they weren't the worst. They just said that we don't want to be part of it. We don't want the American influence. And I'm not anti-American at all, but I think the business model that was fermented in the United States by Bernays and people, and the way that that was rolled out onto the world, has not been a good thing. So it's not like that here. It's such a beautiful city, Lisbon. I still go through areas in Lisbon I've never been through before, and it's just endlessly stunning. It's really, really beautiful. It's light on crime. Policing is very hands-off here, which somehow makes the crime lower. Yeah, it's kind of magical. And of course it's being discovered by other people the whole time, and people love to come here. And a lot of digital nomad types come and live here, people who are able to work like myself, in a way, people whose work is all over the world or online. It's a really great base to be in, a great place to come back to and decompress from the stresses of the modern world, I suppose.

[Unclear audio at 00:20:13–00:20:27]

Lauren: Thanks so much for your time, Pete. I really appreciate it, and thanks for all the music over the years as well.

Pete: My pleasure. Thanks for doing the interview.
